passage: In Class 9 there was the back-bench group, and there was me. Akash and his four friends did everything together: lunch, cricket, the same jokes. When Akash forgot his homework, they said, "Sir gives too much anyway." When one of them copied in the unit test, it was "just helping each other." But when I forgot my lab coat once, Akash announced to the class, "Ujjwal is so careless." When I got a question wrong, they laughed for a full minute. Same mistakes, different rules. I stopped raising my hand. What hurt wasn't only the laughing. It was seeing how gently they treated each other, and knowing I would never get that. That year taught me what loyalty looks like from the outside: a locked door.

qa.q: What did Akash say when Ujjwal forgot the lab coat?
qa.a: "Ujjwal is so careless."

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal feel so hurt that year?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt hurt and shut out, seeing how gently the group treated each other while Ujjwal was judged harshly for the same mistakes.

qa.q: What could a teacher or classmate do if they noticed this pattern?
qa.a: Point out the double standard calmly, apply the same rules to everyone, and bring Ujjwal into group work so the door opens a little.

qa.q: How might Akash's group see their own behaviour?
qa.a: They probably see it as normal loyalty to friends, without noticing how unfair it feels to someone outside.

grounding: A teenager recalls being outside a clique that excused its own members' slips while judging the same slips harshly in the outsider.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 11B, 18 November
Jatin joined us in August from another city and has not been let into any group. This week I noticed a pattern. When Trisha's group came back late from the canteen, the class monitor, who is part of it, wrote nothing. When Jatin came in two minutes late on Wednesday, she wrote his name on the board. During the group presentation, Trisha's friends praised each other's slides and called Jatin's section "confusing," though it was the clearest. He sat very still afterwards and skipped lunch. Today he asked me quietly if he could do the next project alone. I said I would think about it. I will speak to the monitor about applying the late rule equally, and I will set the next groups myself.

qa.q: What did the monitor do when Jatin came in two minutes late?
qa.a: Wrote his name on the board.

qa.q: Why did Jatin ask to do the next project alone?
qa.a: He felt hurt and excluded, seeing the group excuse each other while judging his clear work as confusing.

qa.q: What steps is the teacher taking, and why do they help?
qa.a: Asking the monitor to apply the late rule equally and setting the next groups, so the same rules apply to all and Jatin isn't left outside.

qa.q: How might Trisha's group see their comments on Jatin's section?
qa.a: They may think they were being honest, without noticing they judged him more harshly than their own friends.

grounding: A teacher records a new boy outside a clique being judged harshly for things the group excuses in its own members.

passage:
Sunday night
Two months in the hostel and I've figured out the rules. There's Pema's corridor group, and there's everyone else. When one of them plays music till two, it's "just relaxing." When I played mine at ten, Pema banged on my door and said I had no manners. When their room was messy at inspection, they laughed about it together. When mine had one shirt on the chair, I got called lazy in the corridor.
I'm not even angry today. I'm just tired. It's like they have a softer pair of eyes for each other and a harder one for me.
Tomorrow I'm going to talk to the warden. Not to complain about them. Just to ask if the rules can be written on the board, for everyone.
Chaitanya

qa.q: What did Pema say when Chaitanya played music at ten?
qa.a: That Chaitanya had no manners.

qa.q: How is Chaitanya feeling tonight?
qa.a: Chaitanya feels tired and hurt rather than angry, sensing the group has softer eyes for each other and harder ones for outsiders.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya plan, and why is it a fair step?
qa.a: Asking the warden to write the rules on the board for everyone, which aims at equal rules rather than attacking the group.

qa.q: How might Pema's group see the music and mess rules?
qa.a: They probably see their own behaviour as ordinary relaxing and don't notice they judge Chaitanya by a stricter standard.

grounding: A hostel diary shows an outsider noticing a group excusing its own members while judging the outsider harshly for the same things.

passage:
Monday. On his first day as an intern at the Pune firm, Nilesh noticed that four of the six team members were from the manager's old engineering college. They had in-jokes about a canteen and a professor. Sunaina, the other intern, from a college in Nagpur, laughed along without understanding.
Wednesday. When an interesting client project came up, the manager gave it to the newest intern, from his old college, who had joined a week after Sunaina. Sunaina got the filing. Nilesh watched her face tighten, then smooth over.
Friday. At the weekly feedback session, Nilesh chose his words carefully. "Sir, I've noticed most chances here go to people from one college. Maybe it's accidental. Could we pick projects by the skills listed on our forms?" The room went still. The manager looked at the list of names, then at Sunaina. "That's fair," he said slowly. "Let's do that."

qa.q: What did Sunaina get instead of the client project?
qa.a: The filing.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh choose his words carefully on Friday?
qa.a: He felt nervous about naming the pattern to the manager, but uneasy about Sunaina being passed over, so he framed it gently.

qa.q: What did Nilesh suggest, and why is it a fair first step?
qa.a: Picking projects by the skills on their forms, which names the pattern and gives everyone the same criteria.

qa.q: What might Sunaina have felt on Wednesday?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and overlooked, her face tightening before she hid it.

grounding: Over a week, an intern notices chances flowing to people from the manager's college and names the pattern gently.

passage: Sachin, you're starting hostel life next month, so let your Kishore mama tell you something I saw at twenty. In our engineering hostel, the mess committee was run by boys from one district, and I was one of them. Every good room, every late-night pass, every second helping of paneer went to our own. I didn't think of it as unfair; it just felt like looking after family. Then one evening a quiet boy from far away, Lalthanga, was refused a room change even though his ceiling leaked onto his books. One of our boys, with a dry room, got a change for a better view. I watched Lalthanga carry his wet books down the stairs, and something turned in me. At the next meeting I said it out loud: "We only help our own." Nobody had ever said it. After that we made the room list by need.

qa.q: Why did Lalthanga need a room change?
qa.a: His ceiling leaked onto his books.

qa.q: What did young Kishore feel watching Lalthanga carry his wet books?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and ashamed, suddenly seeing that looking after his own had been unfair to others.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Saying out loud at the meeting, "We only help our own," which named the pattern and led to a room list by need.

qa.q: How might Lalthanga have felt being refused the room change?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and invisible, carrying wet books while a boy with a dry room got a better view.

grounding: An uncle recalls noticing, as a student, that rooms and favours flowed only to boys from his own district, and naming it.

passage: The relief camp had only forty blankets left, rain was still pouring, and the queue stretched to the road. Kishore, a college volunteer, noticed something odd about the list the camp leader was ticking. Most names came from Rampur, the leader's own village, even though the families from the riverbank colony had arrived first and lost more. "We know Rampur people," the leader said when Vidya, another volunteer, asked. "We trust them." Kishore felt his neck prickle; his own family was from Rampur too. He took a breath. "Sir, we're all helping who we know. Could we give blankets in order of arrival, and check who lost their homes?" The leader stared at him, then at the soaked children from the colony. He tore up the list and started again.

qa.q: How many blankets were left?
qa.a: Forty.

qa.q: Why did Kishore feel his neck prickle?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and a little guilty, noticing the favouritism toward Rampur, which was his own family's village too.

qa.q: What did Kishore suggest, and why is it fairer?
qa.a: Giving blankets in order of arrival and checking who lost their homes, so help goes by need rather than by who the leader knows.

qa.q: How might the families from the riverbank colony feel when the list is redone?
qa.a: They would probably feel relieved and finally seen, after arriving first and losing more.

grounding: At a crowded relief camp, a student volunteer notices help flowing to the leader's own village and names the pattern.

passage: Nadia was shortlisting volunteers for the youth centre in Madrid, and two files sat side by side. Laura had gone to Nadia's own university, played in the same orchestra, and wrote an application that felt like a letter from a friend. Pablo had grown up in a small town in the south, left school at sixteen and later finished his diploma at night. Nadia caught herself smiling at Laura's file and frowning at Pablo's spelling. She stopped. She took out her criteria sheet: experience with teenagers, reliability, languages. Pablo had coached a football team for five years and spoke three languages. Laura had tutored once. Then she asked herself: if Pablo had gone to my university, would I be hesitating? She wouldn't. She put both on the interview list, Pablo first.

qa.q: How long had Pablo coached a football team?
qa.a: Five years.

qa.q: What made Nadia stop herself?
qa.a: She caught herself feeling warm toward Laura and doubtful about Pablo for reasons unrelated to the job, and felt uneasy about it.

qa.q: What steps did Nadia use to make a fair call?
qa.a: She used her criteria sheet and asked whether she would hesitate if Pablo had gone to her own university.

qa.q: What might reaching the interview mean for Pablo?
qa.a: It gives him a fair chance based on his real experience, not on shared background with the reviewer.

grounding: A young woman uses clear criteria and asks whether she would decide the same if a candidate were from her own group.

passage: The selection meeting for the school's leadership programme was in the staff room, and Neelam, the youngest coordinator, had the final say for Class 9. Her first list had eight names. She noticed, uncomfortably, that six of them were students she knew well: from her own neighbourhood, or from the debating club she ran. Kashish, a new girl from a government school who barely spoke in class, wasn't on it. Neelam sat back. She wrote the programme's three criteria on a card: shows initiative, helps others, finishes what they start. Then she went through the teachers' notes for every student, not just the ones she knew. Kashish had organised a book swap and tutored two classmates in maths. Neelam asked herself: if Kashish were one of my debaters, would she be on the list? Yes. Kashish went on the list.

qa.q: What had Kashish organised?
qa.a: A book swap.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel when she looked at her first list?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable, noticing that six of the eight names were students she knew well.

qa.q: What did Neelam do to make the list fair?
qa.a: She wrote clear criteria, read the notes on every student, and asked whether Kashish would be included if Kashish were one of her own debaters.

qa.q: What might being picked mean for Kashish?
qa.a: Kashish, new and quiet, might feel seen and encouraged, recognised for real initiative rather than overlooked.

grounding: A young coordinator notices her list favours students she knows, then uses clear criteria and asks if she would decide the same for an outsider.

passage:
Dear Pema,
Before Friday's scholarship meeting, I want to share something I noticed in myself, in case it's useful.
When I read the forty applications last week, I ranked the Pune students higher on "potential" without really knowing why. Then I realised: I'm from Pune. Their essays mentioned places and teachers I know, and it felt like they were my people.
So I re-read all forty using only our three written criteria: marks, need and community work. For each Pune student I also asked: would I give the same score if this student were from Latur or Kohima? Four scores went down. Two students from the northeast went up.
Could we both try this check before Friday? And maybe invite someone from outside our city onto the panel next year?
Warmly,
Pallavi

qa.q: What were the three written criteria?
qa.a: Marks, need and community work.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel on noticing the Pune students ranked higher?
qa.a: Pallavi felt uneasy on realising the essays felt like Pallavi's own people, which had quietly lifted their scores.

qa.q: What check did Pallavi use, and why does it make the choice fairer?
qa.a: Scoring only on the three criteria and asking whether a Pune student would get the same score if from Latur or Kohima, which cancels the pull of the home group.

qa.q: How might Pema react to the letter?
qa.a: Pema might feel appreciative of Pallavi's honesty and willing to try the same check before Friday.

grounding: A young panellist writes about re-scoring applications on clear criteria and checking whether home-town students got an unfair lift.

passage: The storm had knocked out the lights, the classroom was dim, and when the window glass cracked with a bang, Mr Ghosh turned and saw Pallavi standing closest. "Outside! Now!" Pallavi stood in the corridor for the whole period, crying. Bidisha, watching through the door, felt sure: Pallavi must have done something. Teachers don't punish good children. Maybe she had leaned on the glass. Maybe she'd been naughty earlier. "She deserved it," Bidisha whispered to her friend. After lunch the school helper came to fix the window and pointed to a big branch lying on the ledge outside. "The wind did this," he said. Bidisha looked at Pallavi, still red-eyed, and felt her stomach turn. Mr Ghosh called Pallavi in and apologised in front of everyone.

qa.q: What had actually cracked the window?
qa.a: A big branch; the wind did it.

qa.q: Why was Bidisha sure Pallavi deserved the punishment?
qa.a: Bidisha felt reassured believing that teachers only punish bad children, so a fair world made Pallavi seem guilty.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do after learning the truth?
qa.a: Tell Pallavi she's sorry for saying she deserved it, and next time wait for the facts before deciding someone did wrong.

qa.q: What was the period in the corridor like for Pallavi?
qa.a: Pallavi was crying and humiliated, punished for something the wind did.

grounding: A girl assumes a punished classmate must have done something wrong, because the world feels fair, until the real cause appears.

passage: When Kamal's new bicycle was stolen from outside the colony shop in Chennai, Mohit shrugged. "He must have left it unlocked. Bad things happen to careless people." His mother raised an eyebrow but said nothing. Mohit liked believing that; it meant his own cycle, always locked, was safe. On Saturday Kamal's father showed everyone the cut chain. The lock had been fine; a thief with a cutter had taken three cycles from that road the same evening. Mohit stared at the chain. "But Kamal is always careful," he said slowly. "Then why did it happen to him?" "Sometimes bad things just happen," his mother said. "The question is what we do for Kamal now." Mohit thought for a moment, then went to ask Kamal if he wanted to share his cycle for the tuition ride.

qa.q: What did Kamal's father show everyone?
qa.a: The cut chain.

qa.q: Why did Mohit like believing Kamal left the cycle unlocked?
qa.a: It made Mohit feel safe, because if only careless people lose things, his own locked cycle was protected.

qa.q: What did Mohit's mother suggest focusing on?
qa.a: What they could do for Kamal now, instead of deciding whether he deserved it.

qa.q: How might Kamal have felt hearing he must have been careless?
qa.a: Kamal would likely feel hurt and blamed, having locked the cycle properly.

grounding: A boy assumes a friend's stolen cycle means the friend was careless, because believing the world is fair keeps him feeling safe.

passage:
"Rekha aunty lost her job at the factory," said Ujjwal, coming in from the stairs.
Leela didn't look up from her homework. "She must have done something wrong. People don't lose jobs for nothing."
"The whole factory closed, Leela. Two hundred people."
"Then all of them must have been lazy."
"All two hundred?" Ujjwal sat down. "Papa's friend Mani uncle worked there twenty years. Was he lazy?"
Leela frowned. Mani uncle fixed everyone's fans for free and never took a day off. "No."
"So why did it happen?"
"I don't know." Her voice went small. "If it can happen to Mani uncle, can it happen to Papa?"
Ujjwal put an arm round her. "Maybe. That's scary. But blaming Rekha aunty doesn't make it less likely." He picked up a bag. "Mummy made extra rice. Come, let's take it down."

qa.q: How many people worked at the factory?
qa.a: Two hundred people.

qa.q: Why did Leela's voice go small?
qa.a: She felt scared, realising that if it could happen to Mani uncle it could happen to Papa, and that blaming Rekha aunty had been a way to feel safe.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal do that turns the talk toward kindness?
qa.a: He questions the blame gently, admits it's scary, and suggests taking extra rice down to Rekha aunty.

qa.q: How might Rekha aunty feel when they bring the rice?
qa.a: Rekha aunty would probably feel comforted and cared for at a hard time.

grounding: A girl assumes a neighbour lost her job for doing something wrong, until she sees the world is not that fair.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10A, Tuesday
This morning Kavitha told me that a group from another section has been posting mean edited photos of her. I reported it to the school counsellor within the hour, and Kavitha is meeting the counsellor with her parents this afternoon. In class, I overheard Chaitanya telling his friends, "She must have done something to start it. Nobody gets targeted for no reason." When I asked him privately what he meant, he said, "If you keep quiet and don't show off, nobody bothers you." I think he believes this keeps him safe. I explained that people are targeted for all sorts of reasons, and that blaming Kavitha hurts her twice. He looked uncomfortable and said he hadn't thought of it that way. I will run a session on online bullying with the class on Thursday.

qa.q: Who did the teacher report Kavitha's bullying to?
qa.a: The school counsellor, within the hour.

qa.q: Why does Chaitanya believe Kavitha must have started it?
qa.a: He wants to feel safe, so believing that quiet people are never targeted is comforting, even though it blames Kavitha.

qa.q: What did the teacher do for both students?
qa.a: Reported Kavitha's bullying to the counsellor straight away, and privately explained to Chaitanya that blaming her hurts her twice.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel if she heard Chaitanya's comment?
qa.a: She would likely feel hurt again and more alone, as if the bullying were her fault.

grounding: A teacher records a teenage boy blaming a bullied classmate for provoking it, a belief that helps him feel safe.

passage:
Wednesday
Sonali's phone got snatched at the bus stop yesterday. Two guys on a bike. Everyone was being nice to her today, but honestly, what did she expect? She always has it out, scrolling, not looking around. I keep mine in my bag. That's why it won't happen to me.
I said that at lunch, and Sonali just got up and left. Mrs Pinto, who was on lunch duty, called me over. She said Sonali had been holding her phone to check the bus timing, and that the same bike had snatched from an old man and a lady with a bag that week. "Were they showing off too?" I didn't have an answer.
I think I said it because I'm afraid of it being random.
I'm going to say sorry tomorrow.
Suraj

qa.q: Why was Sonali holding her phone, according to Mrs Pinto?
qa.a: To check the bus timing.

qa.q: Why does Suraj think the blame was said at all?
qa.a: Suraj feels afraid of it being random, so believing Sonali caused it made a snatch seem less likely to happen to Suraj.

qa.q: What does Suraj plan, and why is it right?
qa.a: Saying sorry to Sonali tomorrow, because blaming her added hurt to being robbed.

qa.q: How did Sonali react to Suraj's comment?
qa.a: Sonali got up and left, probably hurt and upset to be blamed after being robbed.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows blaming a robbed classmate to feel safe, until a teacher's facts make the blame collapse.

passage:
College counsellor's note, 7 February
Sachin, second year, came in today, brought by his friend Siddharth. He was in hospital with typhoid for three weeks in December and missed his exams. Since coming back, he says, people keep telling him it was his own fault: an uncle said he "must have eaten rubbish from street carts," and a classmate said "weak people fall sick." He has started skipping lunch in the canteen so nobody comments, and he stopped answering the class group. He said, "Maybe they're right. Maybe I did something." I told him clearly that illness is not a punishment and that he did nothing to deserve it. We made a plan for the supplementary exams together, and I will write to his department about extra time. Siddharth will walk with him to the canteen tomorrow.

qa.q: How long was Sachin in hospital?
qa.a: Three weeks in December.

qa.q: Why has Sachin started skipping lunch in the canteen?
qa.a: He feels ashamed and hurt after being told his illness was his own fault, so avoiding people feels safer than hearing more blame.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do, and why does it help?
qa.a: Told Sachin clearly that illness is not a punishment, planned his supplementary exams and asked for extra time, easing both the shame and the practical problem.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel walking with Sachin to the canteen?
qa.a: Siddharth probably feels protective and caring, wanting Sachin to feel less alone.

grounding: A counsellor records a student who, after a long illness, is told he must have deserved it and falls silent in shame.

passage:
Monday night
Results came. Failed thermodynamics. I knew it might happen; my father was in hospital for most of October, and I was at his bedside instead of in class.
But nobody asks about that. My hostel senior said, "Should have studied instead of roaming." A relative on the phone told Amma I must have been "wasting time with friends." Even the professor said, "You get what you work for." Each time I just nodded. What do you even say?
Now I feel like maybe I am lazy. I haven't told anyone how much it hurts.
Tanvir knocked tonight and asked if I'd eaten. I said yes. I hadn't.
Tomorrow maybe I'll tell Tanvir about October.
Tarun

qa.q: Where was Tarun for most of October?
qa.a: At the father's bedside in hospital, instead of in class.

qa.q: How is Tarun feeling after the comments?
qa.a: Tarun feels hurt and ashamed, starting to believe the lazy label, and has told no one how much it hurts.

qa.q: What could help Tarun now?
qa.a: Telling Tanvir, the professor or a counsellor about October, so people understand the real reason and the re-exam can be planned with support.

qa.q: Why might Tanvir have knocked to ask if Tarun had eaten?
qa.a: Tanvir probably noticed Tarun was upset and wanted to check on Tarun gently.

grounding: A student's diary shows people blaming a failed exam on laziness, adding shame and silence to a hard time.

passage: At the IT office in Chennai, the morning after the floods, Akash came in late, in borrowed clothes. His ground-floor flat had filled with water overnight: his books, his laptop, his mother's wedding photos, gone. By the coffee machine someone muttered, "Who rents a ground floor near the river? Should have known." Nazia, his team lead, heard it. She didn't argue at the machine. She went straight to Akash, sat with him and asked what he needed first. Then she moved his deadlines, lent him her spare laptop and started a collection for the three staff who had lost the most. That afternoon she emailed HR: could the company add an emergency leave policy for disasters, so nobody has to depend on luck or a kind lead? "Floods don't check who deserves them," she wrote. "Our rules shouldn't make it worse."

qa.q: What did Nazia lend Akash?
qa.a: Her spare laptop.

qa.q: Why did Nazia go to Akash instead of arguing at the coffee machine?
qa.a: She felt compassion for Akash and knew he needed support more than a debate about blame.

qa.q: How did Nazia both support Akash and work for fairness?
qa.a: She moved his deadlines, lent a laptop and started a collection, then asked HR for an emergency leave policy so others wouldn't depend on luck.

qa.q: How might Akash feel when Nazia asks what he needs first?
qa.a: Akash would likely feel relieved and less alone after losing so much, instead of blamed.

grounding: A young team lead supports a colleague who lost his home in floods without blame, and pushes for a fairer policy.

passage:
Dear Mahima,
I heard about the company shutting your whole department. I'm so sorry. I also heard what some people in the old group chat said, that you "should have seen it coming." Please don't carry that. You worked harder than anyone I know. Sometimes the ground just moves under good people, and it has nothing to do with what they deserve.
What can I do? I can look over your CV this weekend, I can send your name to two teams I know are hiring, or I can just come over with biryani and not talk about jobs at all. You choose.
I've also written to our alumni group asking if we can start a proper referral list for anyone who's laid off, so it isn't just about who knows whom.
With love,
Lavanya

qa.q: What did people in the old group chat say?
qa.a: That Mahima should have seen it coming.

qa.q: How does Lavanya feel about what happened to Mahima?
qa.a: Lavanya feels sad and sorry for Mahima, and protective against the blame from the group chat.

qa.q: How does Lavanya combine support with working for fairness?
qa.a: Offering help with the CV, referrals or simply company, and starting an alumni referral list so help isn't only about who knows whom.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Mahima might feel comforted and less ashamed, with real choices of help and no blame.

grounding: A young woman writes to a laid-off friend without blame, offers support and works for a fairer referral system.

passage: Hansa, you know the tailor's shop at the corner of our market, Iqbal chacha's? It burned down last week. Wiring fault. And you know what I heard at the tea stall? "He must have done something wrong. Things like this don't happen for nothing." I was so angry I couldn't drink my tea. Iqbal chacha is the man who stitched my school uniforms for free when Papa lost his job. So this is what Sudha did. First, I went to his house with dinner and just sat with him and his wife. No speeches. Then I got four of us to help clear the shop. And then I went to the market association and asked why the wiring in that row hadn't been checked in fifteen years. They're checking every shop now. Fires don't ask who's good, Hansa. We can still fix the wires.

passage: In Class 9, my father couldn't afford a new school bag, so I carried my cousin's old one: bright orange, with a cartoon duck on the front. I was sure the whole school stared at it. I walked with it held behind my back. I skipped the inter-school science fair, which I had wanted to go to for months, because we'd have to carry our bags on the bus and I imagined forty people seeing the duck. Mahima, my lab partner, went and came back with a medal. Years later I asked her if she remembered my orange bag. She thought hard. "You had an orange bag?" That was it. The duck I had hidden for a whole year, the reason I missed the fair, nobody had noticed. I still think about that. Arnab and the invisible duck.

qa.a: Arnab felt anxious and embarrassed, sure forty people would stare at the orange duck bag on the bus.
